title: What goes in a UGC script for a skincare brand?
description: What a UGC script for a skincare brand needs: a hook built on a skin situation, the routine, texture on camera, an honest timeline, and the claims to leave out.
short_answer: A skincare UGC script shows the product in a real routine and promises nothing you have not seen yourself. It opens on a skin situation the viewer recognises, gives the texture a close-up, says honestly how long you have used it, and closes by asking for one thing.

sections.heading: Why is a skincare UGC script harder to write than most?

blocks.text: Skincare results are slow and vary by person, so a skincare script sells what the camera can see today.

A gadget can be shown working in one take. A moisturiser can't, and a video that pretends otherwise asks the viewer to believe something you haven't filmed. What a camera can show is the texture on a fingertip, how much you use, where the product sits between cleanser and sunscreen, and how your skin looks straight after you put it on.

A skincare brief may also come with words you must use and words you must never say. That list wins over anything that sounds better, so read it before you write the hook. [How to turn a brand brief into a script](/blog/brief-to-script/) shows how to mark what is fixed and what is yours.

sections.heading: What should the hook of a skincare UGC video be about?

blocks.text: The hook should name a skin situation the viewer is in right now, not a result the product might give them.

A result hook makes a promise the rest of the video can't keep, and a brief that bans result claims won't allow it anyway. A situation hook is true for you and familiar to the viewer, and it sets the product up as the next step in a routine rather than a miracle. The shapes in [how to write a UGC hook that stops the scroll](/how-to-write-a-hook/) all work here, as long as the [hook](/glossary/#hook) points at the situation.

table_rows: “My skin feels tight by lunch, whatever I put on in the morning.”
“I've been using three products where I think I need one.”
“This is what my cheeks look like under makeup by the afternoon.”
“I keep buying creams that feel nice in the jar and greasy by noon.”

sections.heading: What beats does a skincare UGC script need?

blocks.text: A skincare UGC script needs five beats: the situation, the routine, the texture, an honest timeline, and a close that asks for one thing.

Each [beat](/glossary/#beat) should change what's on screen, so the viewer always has something new to look at while you talk. The parts are the same ones laid out in [the parts of a UGC video script](/short-form-script-structure/); skincare only fixes what goes in each.

table_rows: You name the skin situation, with your bare skin in frame.
Makes the viewer check their own skin.
You show where the product sits: after cleanser, before sunscreen, or wherever the brief says.
A close shot of the product on a fingertip, then on skin.
You say how long you've used it, in plain words.
You ask for one thing: the link, a save or a comment.
Gives the viewer a next step.

blocks.text: In this shape the [turn](/glossary/#the-turn) is the texture shot. It's the moment the product stops being a jar in your hand and becomes something the viewer can almost feel, so keep it close, keep it slow, and don't talk over all of it.

sections.heading: Which claims should a skincare UGC script leave out?

blocks.text: Leave out any claim about what the product does to skin unless you have seen it yourself or the brief gives it word for word.

items: Medical words. Treatment language isn't yours to use. Say what you noticed instead: “My skin felt less tight by the end of the week.”
Promises about other people. You know your skin, not everyone's. Say who you are: “I have combination skin, and it didn't make my forehead shiny.”
A staged before-and-after. If the brief asks for one, film both halves in the same light, at the same angle, after the time has really passed.
Ingredient explanations. If the brief names an ingredient, use the brief's words exactly and don't add what it does.

blocks.text: Every one of these is a [UGC](/glossary/#ugc) habit worth keeping on any product, but skincare is where a careless line does the most harm: the viewer is deciding what to put on their face. When a line sits between what you've seen and what the brand wants said, follow the brief.

sections.heading: What does a finished skincare UGC script look like?

blocks.text: Here is a full script for a lightweight gel moisturiser, written for a creator with combination skin who has used it for two weeks.

blocks.script_caption: Example script — written for this answer, for a lightweight gel moisturiser

script_beats.say: By lunch my skin feels tight, and by the afternoon it's shiny. Same face, same day.
script_beats.do: Close on your face by a window in daylight, no makeup, fingertips on one cheek.

script_beats.say: I was fixing it with two products: a heavy cream in the morning and blotting papers all afternoon.
script_beats.do: Hold up a thick cream and a pack of blotting papers, then put both down out of frame.

script_beats.say: Two weeks ago I swapped the cream for this.
script_beats.do: Pick the gel moisturiser up off the bathroom shelf, next to your cleanser.

script_beats.say: It's a gel, so it goes on cool and sinks in instead of sitting on top.
script_beats.do: Squeeze a little onto a fingertip close to the lens, then spread it across one cheek.

script_beats.say: Cleanser, this, sunscreen. That's my whole morning now.
script_beats.do: Three quick shots: cleanser, moisturiser, sunscreen, then the bottles lined up on the shelf.

script_beats.say: The afternoon shine is what I noticed first. If your skin does the tight-then-shiny thing too, the one I use is linked.
script_beats.do: Later in the day, back by the window, tilt your face to the light, then point down at the caption.

blocks.text: Every line in it is something the creator saw or did, which is why it holds up: a viewer with the same skin recognises their own afternoon, and nothing asks them to believe more than you saw. Only film the close if it's true after your own two weeks. If your skin didn't change, cut its first sentence and end on the routine. For the template underneath it, see [a UGC script template that holds up](/ugc-script-template/).
